title: Transparent Hugepage Compaction Stalls
exclusions: This host-level monitor does not measure stall duration, identify the stalled process, prove which huge-page allocation caused a stall, or prescribe a kernel tuning change. The counters are unavailable when the relevant kernel features are not built, and absence of an alert does not establish healthy application latency. Per-process attribution requires separate tracing; compliance and security conclusions are outside scope.
evidence: Searchable evidence is the raw `linux:proc_vmstat:thp` snapshot series plus the result rows retained from saved search `linux_thp_compaction_stalls`. Each result records the host, boot ID, window bounds, sample count, compaction counter deltas, and contextual collapse-allocation outcomes. These artefacts demonstrate counter movement only; they do not demonstrate stall duration or process-level causality.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a test index, load at least two ordered `linux:proc_vmstat:thp` snapshots for the same `host` and `boot_id` with `collector_status=ok`. Between snapshots, increase `compact_stall` from 100 to 101 without decreasing any other required counter; the THP collapse counters may remain unchanged. Run the calculation pipeline over that interval and confirm one row with `compact_stall_delta=1`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Repeat the test with the same valid fields but leave `compact_stall` unchanged while increasing `thp_collapse_alloc_failed`; the final `where` clause must return no row because a collapse allocation failure is not itself a measured process stall. Also verify that different `boot_id` values, decreasing counters, `collector_status=unsupported`, or only one sample do not produce an alert.

dataSources: A custom scripted input reads cumulative event counters from Linux `/proc/vmstat` every 60 seconds into `index=os` with `sourcetype=linux:proc_vmstat:thp`. Required event fields are `collector_status`, `boot_id`, `compact_stall`, `compact_fail`, `compact_success`, `thp_collapse_alloc`, and `thp_collapse_alloc_failed`; Splunk supplies `_time` and `host`. The compaction fields require a kernel built with `CONFIG_COMPACTION`, while the THP fields require `CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE`.
app: A deployment app containing a custom scripted input for the Splunk Universal Forwarder and matching sourcetype settings for the parsing and search tiers; no Splunkbase or premium app is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux:proc_vmstat:thp collector_status=ok
| fields _time host boot_id compact_stall compact_fail compact_success thp_collapse_alloc thp_collapse_alloc_failed
| eval compact_stall=tonumber(compact_stall), compact_fail=tonumber(compact_fail), compact_success=tonumber(compact_success), thp_collapse_alloc=tonumber(thp_collapse_alloc), thp_collapse_alloc_failed=tonumber(thp_collapse_alloc_failed)
| where isnotnull(host) AND isnotnull(boot_id) AND isnotnull(compact_stall) AND isnotnull(compact_fail) AND isnotnull(compact_success) AND isnotnull(thp_collapse_alloc) AND isnotnull(thp_collapse_alloc_failed)
| sort 0 host boot_id _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(compact_stall) AS previous_compact_stall last(compact_fail) AS previous_compact_fail last(compact_success) AS previous_compact_success last(thp_collapse_alloc) AS previous_thp_collapse_alloc last(thp_collapse_alloc_failed) AS previous_thp_collapse_alloc_failed BY host boot_id
| where isnotnull(previous_compact_stall) AND compact_stall>=previous_compact_stall AND compact_fail>=previous_compact_fail AND compact_success>=previous_compact_success AND thp_collapse_alloc>=previous_thp_collapse_alloc AND thp_collapse_alloc_failed>=previous_thp_collapse_alloc_failed
| eval compact_stall_delta=compact_stall-previous_compact_stall, compact_fail_delta=compact_fail-previous_compact_fail, compact_success_delta=compact_success-previous_compact_success, thp_collapse_alloc_delta=thp_collapse_alloc-previous_thp_collapse_alloc, thp_collapse_failed_delta=thp_collapse_alloc_failed-previous_thp_collapse_alloc_failed
| stats sum(compact_stall_delta) AS compact_stall_delta sum(compact_fail_delta) AS compact_fail_delta sum(compact_success_delta) AS compact_success_delta sum(thp_collapse_alloc_delta) AS thp_collapse_alloc_delta sum(thp_collapse_failed_delta) AS thp_collapse_failed_delta count AS sample_intervals earliest(_time) AS window_start latest(_time) AS window_end BY host boot_id
| eval compaction_attempt_delta=compact_fail_delta+compact_success_delta, compaction_failure_pct=if(compaction_attempt_delta>0,round(100*compact_fail_delta/compaction_attempt_delta,2),null()), thp_collapse_attempt_delta=thp_collapse_alloc_delta+thp_collapse_failed_delta, thp_collapse_failure_pct=if(thp_collapse_attempt_delta>0,round(100*thp_collapse_failed_delta/thp_collapse_attempt_delta,2),null())
| where compact_stall_delta>0
| convert ctime(window_start) ctime(window_end)
| table host boot_id window_start window_end sample_intervals compact_stall_delta compact_fail_delta compact_success_delta compaction_failure_pct thp_collapse_alloc_delta thp_collapse_failed_delta thp_collapse_failure_pct
description: Detects Linux hosts where the cumulative `compact_stall` counter increases during the search window, meaning one or more processes stalled to run memory compaction for a huge page. It reports per-boot deltas and contextual compaction and collapse-allocation outcomes while preventing reboots or counter resets from becoming false increases.
value: Direct memory compaction can delay allocating processes, while collapse-allocation outcomes add context about the kernel's ability to obtain contiguous memory for requested large pages. Surfacing these stalls shortens latency triage and supports workload-aware tuning, reducing the risk of recurring performance incidents without claiming more precision than the counters provide.
implementation: Deploy the provided read-only `/proc/vmstat` collector at a 60-second interval, verify all required counters on each kernel, then schedule the delta search over complete 15-minute windows. Start with any same-window increase as an investigative signal and establish host-class baselines before attaching paging severity or changing kernel policy.
visualization: A results table keyed by host and boot ID, plus time-series panels for `compact_stall_delta`, `thp_collapse_failed_delta`, `compaction_failure_pct`, and `thp_collapse_failure_pct`. Show unsupported collectors in a separate data-quality single value; do not chart cumulative raw counters as rates.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **`stress-ng` or an application load test using large pages** — An approved performance test can intentionally create genuine but expected compaction stalls. Confirm the test command and host scope in the change record, then record a time-bound exception in alert routing keyed to that host and only the approved test window.

2. **Database or Java service warm-up after a deployment** — Rapid heap population can create a short-lived burst that is expected for that release. Correlate the result with the deployment timestamp and application latency; suppress paging during the documented warm-up window, but retain the result for baseline review.

3. **A transparent-hugepage policy rollout under production load** — Changing the host's defragmentation policy can alter direct-compaction behavior while applications continue allocating memory. Verify the active value under `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/`, the configuration-management change, and its maintenance window; use a time-bounded maintenance mute and compare before/after latency before accepting the new baseline.

4. **A real host-level stall with no user-visible impact** — `/proc/vmstat` has no process, duration, or allocation identifier, so a short stall in a non-critical workload can be operationally harmless. Distinguish it with application latency telemetry and, when attribution is required, a short controlled trace of `__alloc_pages()` plus the `mm_page_alloc` tracepoint as described by the kernel documentation. Keep the alert investigative or require repeated windows for paging.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux memory-performance monitoring; no security technique asserted)
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites

Use a Linux kernel that exposes all five required counters in `/proc/vmstat`. The Linux THP documentation defines `compact_stall`, `compact_fail`, `compact_success`, `thp_collapse_alloc`, and `thp_collapse_alloc_failed`; the kernel source places the compaction names behind `CONFIG_COMPACTION` and the THP names behind `CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE`. Check availability with `awk '$1 ~ /^(compact_stall|compact_fail|compact_success|thp_collapse_alloc|thp_collapse_alloc_failed)$/ {print}' /proc/vmstat`; exactly five lines must be returned. `/proc/vmstat` is normally readable without elevated privileges, so run the collector as the Splunk service account and do not grant root solely for this use case. A Universal Forwarder must already send to an indexer, and the `os` index must exist with suitable role access. No CIM model, Splunkbase add-on, premium app, debugfs mount, network API, or kernel debug logging is required.

Step 1 — Configure data collection

Package `collect_thp_vmstat.sh` from `scriptExample` in a deployment app as `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_thp_vmstat/bin/collect_thp_vmstat.sh`, owned by the forwarder account and executable. Add this stanza to the app's `local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://./bin/collect_thp_vmstat.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
sourcetype = linux:proc_vmstat:thp
```

On the parsing tier, set `SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false` and `DATETIME_CONFIG=CURRENT` for `[linux:proc_vmstat:thp]` because each script run emits one event without an embedded timestamp. On the search tier, retain `KV_MODE=auto` for that sourcetype so the emitted `name=value` pairs become the fields used by the SPL. Distribute these settings through the deployment mechanism appropriate to each Splunk tier; do not assume a forwarder-only app supplies search-time extraction.

Deploy the input only to Linux forwarders. The script emits one key-value event per host per poll, or 1,440 events per host per day at 60 seconds. It reads cumulative counters and a boot ID; it does not write to `/proc` or `/sys`. `collector_status=unsupported` means at least one required counter is absent, which is a coverage finding rather than a zero value. Keep that event and exclude it from the performance search. Splunk adds `_time` and `host`; the configured key-value extraction supplies the remaining fields. Confirm `boot_id` is populated and that all counter fields parse as non-negative integers. Do not substitute `/sys/kernel/debug/thp_collapse_alloc`: that path is not the documented source for these counters.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Save the `spl` field as `linux_thp_compaction_stalls`. Run every 15 minutes, delayed for ingestion, for example cron `5,20,35,50 * * * *` with earliest `-20m@m` and latest `-5m@m`. The query sorts snapshots within each host and boot ID, obtains the prior sample with `streamstats`, rejects missing or decreasing values, and sums adjacent differences. Grouping by `boot_id` prevents a reboot from comparing a new counter epoch with the previous boot. The two percentages are ratios of event-count deltas: they are not elapsed time, pages, bytes, or CPU percentage.

Understanding this SPL and thresholds: the final condition requires `compact_stall_delta>0`, which means the documented stall counter increased at least once in the window. The collapse-allocation deltas are context and are not required to fire because a collapse failure is not itself a measured process stall. The kernel documentation defines what increments each counter but does not publish a universal healthy threshold, so this deliberately sensitive rule is an investigative starting point, not a vendor severity boundary. Run the reporting portion without the final `where` for at least seven representative days, split baselines by workload class, and record typical per-window deltas before promoting the search to paging. If routine bursts are expected, require repeated affected windows or a corroborating application-latency condition in a separate correlation search; do not relabel event counts as milliseconds.

Step 3 — Validate

First, compare a raw event with the same host's `/proc/vmstat` output within one poll interval; the five integer values and `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` must match. Second, use `index=os sourcetype=linux:proc_vmstat:thp | timechart span=5m count by host limit=0` over 24 hours to find collection gaps; at a 60-second interval each continuously connected host should normally contribute about five events per bucket, allowing for forwarding delay. Third, run the positive and negative `controlTest` cases in a test index or with an equivalent `makeresults` harness. Confirm that collapse-only movement does not alert, a changed boot ID does not bridge snapshots, and a decreasing counter is discarded. Finally, inspect `collector_status` by host and investigate every `unsupported` or `unreadable` value instead of converting it to zero. Do not force production compaction merely to prove the alert; synthetic counter snapshots exercise the SPL without risking workload latency.

Step 4 — Operationalize

Place alert rows in a Linux memory-health dashboard beside application p95/p99 latency, memory pressure, swap activity, and deployment annotations. Retain raw snapshots long enough to cover the baseline and incident-review period defined by local policy. Route the initial saved search to the platform-performance queue, throttle duplicate notifications by host for 60 minutes, and require an operator to confirm user-visible latency before escalating. The first runbook actions are to confirm source continuity and boot ID, identify an active load test or deployment, compare `compact_fail_delta` with `compact_success_delta`, and review the THP policy under `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/` without changing it. Kernel policy changes can trade throughput, memory use, and latency; test them on the affected workload and use change control.

Step 5 — Troubleshoot

No event from one host: verify the deployment app reached that forwarder, the script is executable, and the forwarder account can read `/proc/vmstat`. `collector_status=unsupported`: check the five-line prerequisite command and the running kernel configuration; do not fabricate absent counters. Empty numeric fields: inspect the raw event and confirm the sourcetype still performs key-value extraction. Large negative differences after reboot: confirm `boot_id` is present and included in both `streamstats` and `stats`; negative pairs are intentionally rejected. Duplicate timestamps or zero deltas: check for duplicate scripted-input stanzas and use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` on the forwarder. Missing recent samples: compare the scripted-input runtime with the 60-second interval and inspect forwarder internal logs for script timeout or forwarding backlog. Alerts with no application impact: this can be valid because event counts contain no duration; keep the result for trend review, use tracing only during a controlled diagnostic window, and tune paging from measured workload baselines rather than an invented global limit.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for times when a Linux server pauses a program so it can reorganize memory for a large page. This helps the operations team investigate slow applications without pretending the counter reveals which program paused or for how long.
scriptExample:
#!/bin/sh
# Read-only collector for cumulative Linux VM event counters.
VMSTAT=/proc/vmstat
BOOT_ID_FILE=/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id

if [ ! -r "$VMSTAT" ]; then
  printf '%s\n' 'collector_status=unreadable metric_source=proc_vmstat'
  exit 0
fi

boot_id=unknown
if [ -r "$BOOT_ID_FILE" ]; then
  IFS= read -r boot_id < "$BOOT_ID_FILE"
fi

awk -v boot_id="$boot_id" '
BEGIN {
  wanted["compact_stall"] = 1
  wanted["compact_fail"] = 1
  wanted["compact_success"] = 1
  wanted["thp_collapse_alloc"] = 1
  wanted["thp_collapse_alloc_failed"] = 1
}
($1 in wanted) { value[$1] = $2 }
END {
  status = "ok"
  for (name in wanted) {
    if (!(name in value)) status = "unsupported"
  }
  printf "collector_status=%s metric_source=proc_vmstat boot_id=%s", status, boot_id
  if ("compact_stall" in value) printf " compact_stall=%s", value["compact_stall"]
  if ("compact_fail" in value) printf " compact_fail=%s", value["compact_fail"]
  if ("compact_success" in value) printf " compact_success=%s", value["compact_success"]
  if ("thp_collapse_alloc" in value) printf " thp_collapse_alloc=%s", value["thp_collapse_alloc"]
  if ("thp_collapse_alloc_failed" in value) printf " thp_collapse_alloc_failed=%s", value["thp_collapse_alloc_failed"]
  printf "\n"
}' "$VMSTAT"
